# Almost Everything Is Forgotten

There is a shoebox in my closet full of photographs that belong to no one. They came from an estate sale, decades compressed into cardboard: women in aprons squinting into the sun, a man holding up a fish like a trophy, a birthday party blurred mid-laugh. In one picture a young woman is laughing so hard she has to lean on somebody's shoulder—and whoever that shoulder belonged to didn't make it into the frame, or did and was cropped out by the camera's indifferent hunger. She is radiant. Her name went wherever names go. Whoever loved her enough to take the picture, and to develop it, and to keep it, is gone too, and their grieving and their keeping ended in a shoebox priced at three dollars.

We tend to talk about forgetting as failure, a malfunction, a betrayal. But it's worth stating plainly: almost everything is forgotten. This is the default setting of the universe. Almost every leaf that ever fell in every forest fell without witnesses and rotted without record. Almost every creature that ever lived left no fossil at all—soft bodies dissolve, bones scatter, and the fossil record is a rounding error atop a catastrophe of disappearance. More than a hundred billion humans have been born, by reasonable estimates, and the number whose names survive is laughably, lyrically small. Your descendants will not know your middle name. They may not know your face. This is not pessimism. It is arithmetic.

Languages test the theory most brutally. Depending on who is counting, a language dies every few weeks or every few months, which means that entire ways of describing rain, grief, distant relatives, and the specific blue of an afternoon blink out continuously. When Boa Senior, the last speaker of the Bo language of the Andaman Islands, died in 2010, the linguists who had worked with her reported that she still sang the old songs—and that the words of those songs were now meaningless to every living person. She carried them faithfully for years to an audience of zero. There is something both devastating and noble in that image, of a woman singing into the dark on behalf of everyone who had already slipped through it.

And yet the opposite condition would be unbearable. Borges imagined a man named Funes who, after an accident, could forget nothing. Every leaf, every change of light, every version of his own face in the mirror occupied him with total, crushing fidelity. Funes barely managed to think, because thinking *is* a kind of forgetting—to generalize is to let particulars blur, to hold the idea of *dog* by releasing the seventeen thousand dogs you've met. Forgetting is editing, and editing is mercy. The fever of childhood dims. The grudge softens into anecdote. Sleep runs a nightly amnesty. Every morning you wake up slightly rearranged, lighter than the day deserves.

Which makes our current moment strange. We are the first generations who archive compulsively rather than selectively. Forty thousand photographs in the cloud. Screenshots of screenshots. Videos of meals nobody would order twice. But storage is not memory; a warehouse is not a mind. Nobody looks at those pictures again—the retrieval fails long before the retention does—and so we accumulate data centers that function less like libraries than like climate-controlled catacombs, storing our trivia against our interest in it. Earlier eras had forgetting done for them by the patient labor of time. Ours may be the first that has to practice it on purpose, deliberately, like breathing exercises: let the night go undocumented. Let the moment exist only because you were inside it. It counts. It counted more, probably.

Still, knowing the flood wins, we stack our pebbles anyway, and this seems to me one of the most stubbornly lovable things about people. A grandmother writes her recipe for stew on the back of a calendar page, and it survives four more generations if it's lucky. A medieval mason carves his mark into a joint of stone that no living eye will find, high in the roof tracery where only God and pigeons congregate. Lovers scratch initials into wet cement, which is possibly humanity's most succinct thesis statement about mortality: *we were here, briefly, alphabetically.* In secondhand books I find strangers' marginalia—someone named presumably, arguing with Tolstoy in pencil in 1974, insisting he's wrong about Anna—and that penciled outrage has outlasted, so far, the person who felt it. None of these gestures defeats forgetting. All of them answer it.

So I take the laughing woman out of the shoebox again. Archaeology of the anonymous has limits; she will not be recovered. But memory, whenever it survives, never survives purely anyway—it always arrives carrying luggage full of invention. So I caption her myself, tenderly, the way family does. Call her Vera. Let her be the one who told inappropriate jokes at funerals and got away with it because everyone needed it. Somebody sat across from her at kitchen tables. Somebody watched that exact laugh happen more than once and considered it an amenity of being alive. If the record won't say so, then a stranger with a pen will, and maybe that fabrication is just loyalty wearing a disguise—the only format available to us.

The box goes back on the shelf. I keep one print of her, tacked above my desk, where I will see her laugh until eventually I won't, and then someone clearing out this room will pin her to their own invented biography, on and on down the line, until paper yellows to translucence and gives out. That's fine. Truly. Impermanence isn't a verdict; it's weather. Nothing was ever going to be kept forever, and the absence of a promise of permanence is strangely freeing—it means today doesn't have to justify itself to eternity, only to itself.

We were never guaranteed to be remembered. We were only ever offered the chance to notice. Look at each other while the light holds. Say the names out loud. Sing the song even if no one understands the words. That's the whole fragile, ancient job description, and everyone who ever loved anyone has held it.

message.reasoning:
The request is open-ended: "Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words." This is a creative invitation. I should write something genuinely interesting, thoughtful, and worth reading—something that showcases what free writing can be when it's actually given care.

What should I write about? I have a few options:
1. A personal essay / reflective piece on some topic I find genuinely interesting
2. A short story or piece of fiction
3. A meditation on something specific—memory, time, language, the ocean, cities, sleep, whatever
4. Something meta about the nature of the request itself (but this risks being clever-but-hollow)

I think the best move is to write something with genuine intellectual and aesthetic texture—an essayistic piece that roams a bit, which suits "write freely" well. Free writing suggests movement, digression, following threads. An essay that begins somewhere concrete and wanders productively feels right.

Let me brainstorm topics that could sustain 1000 words of genuinely engaging prose:

- The phenomenology of night — what happens to the mind at 3am
- Libraries as spaces
- The strangeness of handwriting
- Rain and memory
- The idea of "elsewhere" — how humans invented places they'd never seen (maps, Atlases)
- Repetition — why we re-read books, revisit places
- Time perception — why summers felt endless in childhood
- The lyricism of ordinary objects — keys, teaspoons
- The sea / deep time
- Waiting rooms, thresholds, transitional spaces
- The voices we hear when reading

One rich vein: the strange fact that most of our lives are spent in mundane interludes but memory only keeps the highlights. Or: liminal spaces.

Another: what happens in the moment before sleep. Hypnagogia. That's vivid and relatable.

Or something about how a place changes when you learn its history—walking through a city with layered knowledge.

Actually, let me consider writing about "dead malls," "the last speaker of a language," "the sound of the refrigerator at night"—small concrete things that open onto big themes. The best essays start small and open outward.

Let me try: an essay about the hour before dawn, or about forgotten things—the enormous proportion of everything that is forgotten. Forgetting as the default state of the universe. That's fertile: personal forgetting, cultural forgetting, geological, even physical entropy. And there's a counter-theme: memory as effortful exception, meaning as something carved against the grain of oblivion. It could land emotionally without being saccharine.

Alternatively, write fiction—a vignette. But free-writing essay feels more honest to the prompt, like thinking on the page.

Let me draft mentally:

Opening: Start concrete—finding an old photograph, or noticing you've forgotten someone's name, or opening a box of cassette tapes labeled in handwriting that isn't quite yours anymore. Then expand: forgetting is not failure but the norm; memory exists against an ocean of loss; every act of remembering is rare and slightly miraculous; cultures forget too—whole languages gone in a generation; species, towns, names of streets. Then pivot: forgetting does work—it edits, mercifully, makes room; Borges' Funes; the mercy of dimming. End: the photograph goes back in the box, but you keep one detail; the small defiance of writing things down, telling stories, naming things—which is all anyone has ever done against the dark. Something like that.

Let me be careful about tone: warm, precise, a little wry, not purple. Avoid clichés ("passage of time," "march of progress"). Use fresh images. Vary sentence rhythm. Include specifics—dates, names, textures—to make it feel lived-in rather than abstract.

Concrete anchors I might use:
- A shoebox of photographs, uncaptioned, someone else's memories
- Grandmother's kitchen, a specific smell (cardamom? burned toast?)
- Names: most people who ever lived are unremembered; population estimates (~117 billion humans ever born), nearly all names lost
- Dead languages: one dies roughly every few months by some estimates; a language dying with its last speaker—e.g., the concept, maybe reference Boa Sr. (last speaker of Aka-Bo, died 2010) — I know this fairly confidently; she died in 2010 on the Andaman Islands, and reports said she sang songs no one understood.
- Funes the Memorious—Borges, remembering everything as a curse
- The forgetting curve of Ebbinghaus
- Digital hoarding paradox—we save everything now and therefore curate nothing; screenshots as琥珀?
- Geology: most creatures left no fossils; fossils are vanishingly rare exceptions
- Light from dead stars—not quite relevant; skip
- The smell of a book, marginalia from a used book—you get a stranger's notes, remembering their reading

Structure sketch:
1. Cold open: photograph in a box, unknown people, joy unattributable. ~120 words
2. Claim: forgetting is the default; memory is the anomaly. Expand to human scale—billions of lives, namelessness. ~180 words
3. Languages and last speakers. ~150 words
4. Funes / the case for forgetting: mercy, editing, the self as story requires cuts. ~150 words
5. Modern twist: we now archive compulsively; does storage equal memory? The cloud will outlive our interest in it; hard drives as catacombs. ~150 words
6. Small resistances: recipes passed down, marginalia, teaching a child a song, stone-cutters signing cathedrals secretly, writing names in wet cement. ~150 words
7. Close: return to the photo. Put it back. But copy down a caption guess, invent a tenderness—remembering is partly making. Final line lands quiet. ~100 words

That totals ~1000 words. Good.

Facts to keep accurate-ish:
- ~117 billion humans ever born (PRB estimate). I can say "over a hundred billion."
- Boa Sr., died February 2010, last fluent speaker of Aka-Bo (Great Andamanese), reportedly in her 80s. She sang songs in the language; linguists noted she sang songs whose words no one living understood. That's widely reported. Safe enough with soft framing ("by the accounts of the linguists who knew her").
- Funes el memorioso: Ireneo Funes, after accident, remembers everything; Borges suggests thinking is abstraction/forgetting—"To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions." Good.
- Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: steep initial drop. Can mention lightly without numbers.
- Cathedral masons' marks: stonemasons did carve marks; some artisans signed hidden places. Fine.
- Amnesiac Henry Molaison (H.M.)—couldn't form new memories; famously lived in a 20-second loop. Could use but maybe skip for space.

Now think about style: first person, essay voice. Sentences varied; some short. Concrete nouns. Minimal hedging. Some rhetorical turns but not overdone. Em dashes sparingly. No bullet points obviously—this is prose.

Length target: ~1000 words. I'll aim between 950–1050. I should count approximately as I go. Paragraphs of moderate length; maybe 8–10 paragraphs.

Draft:

Title? Could add one— "In Praise of Losing Things" or "Everything Is Forgotten (and What We Do Anyway)". A title is a nice touch. Maybe "The Box of Uncaptioned Photographs"? Simpler: "On Forgetting". Or "Most of Everything Vanishes". Let me choose "Everything Is Forgotten, and Yet" — hmm. "What the Dark Keeps". I'll go with something simple: "A Defense of Forgetting" — but the essay complicates defense; it's both defense and elegy. "The Mercy and the Theft" ? Maybe just begin without heavy titling—but a title adds polish. "Almost Everything Is Forgotten" — declarative, fits. Yes.

Let me write.

---

Almost Everything Is Forgotten

Open paragraph:
"In a shoebox..." describe photos: 1940s-60s faces, a woman laughing at someone off-frame, a beach scene, nobody knows who. The person who chose to keep them is gone; choice was made for them by estate sale / house clearance. Their laughter persists without a name attached. That's a good hook.

Second paragraph: extend claim—forgetting is the rule of the universe. Most leaves that fell in forests—not recorded. Most creatures left no fossil—soft bodies dissolve; fossil record is a rounding error. Over 100 billion humans have lived; only a handful remembered. Your great-great-grandchildren won't know your middle name, likely not your face. Memory: exception that proves the rule... Actually "exception that proves the rule" is cliché—rephrase: Remembering is the aberration, and costly: brains spend energy; what is kept must be earned/selected.

Third: languages. One language dies every few months (some estimates say every two weeks historically; more recent estimates say about one every three months—I'll phrase loosely: "somebody's estimate"). Use Boa Sr.: February 2010, Andaman Islands, last speaker of Aka-Bo; news said she sang songs in that language, old songs, and the words meant nothing to anyone alive. She carried them anyway. Beautiful image.

Fourth: the counterpoint—Borges' Funes. He fell from a horse, gained perfect memory, was crushed by totality. To think is to forget: generalization, abstraction. Forgetting as editing, grace, kindness. Childhood fevers fade; grudges soften into anecdotes. Sleep as nightly amnesty. Maybe: every morning you wake slightly rearranged.

Fifth: the modern paradox. We archive indiscriminately now—clouds, screenshots, 40,000 photos. Storage ≠ memory. Nobody has ever looked at those photos again. Data centers as climate-controlled catacombs. Forgetting required a servant before (the passage of years); now we must practice it deliberately—or drown. The liberty of letting a night go undocumented.

Sixth: small resistances. Against the vast default, tiny acts: a grandmother's recipe written on the back of a calendar page; a child taught a lullaby that will survive four more generations if lucky; medieval masons carving marks where no eye would find them; lovers scratching initials in wet cement—graffiti as thesis statement about mortality. Marginalia in secondhand books: stranger arguing with Tolstoy in pencil, 1974. Each is a pebble stacked against tide, aware it will lose, doing it anyway.

Seventh: return to the box. Take the laughing woman out again. You cannot recover her; archaeology of the negligible fails. So do the one thing memory always smuggles: invention. Caption her anyway—invented tenderly: call her Aunt Vera; let her be the one who told jokes at funerals. Insist: we were here, someone laughed until she had to sit down. The fabrication is a kind of loyalty.

Close: put lid back on box; keep one photo on the fridge / tacked above desk. It will outlast your certainty about her. Eventually it too—someone's garage sale, etc. And that's fine: forgetfulness keeps the door open; impermanence means endings are not verdicts, just weather. Final line: something like "We were never promised to be kept. Only, sometimes, to notice. That's the whole fragile job: to look at each other while there's light, and say so."

Word budget check per para: 110 + 150 + 130 + 140 + 140 + 150 + 130 + 90 ≈ 1040. Fine.

Now watch language quality: avoid "tapestry," "journey," "delve," "testament," "symphony." Keep verbs active. Sensory specificity. Some humor lightly sprinkled (screenshots of screenshots, "1,247 unread notifications as proof of life").

Formatting: This is creative prose—one flowing piece with paragraphs, optional title in italics or bold. Markdown fine since chat renders it. Title as heading maybe. No lists. Good.

Let me also double-check factual claims for safety:
- "Over a hundred billion humans have ever been born": PRB estimate ~117 billion; safe.
- Boa Sr death Feb 2010, Port Blair, Andaman Islands; last speaker of Bo (Aka-Bo), one of Great Andamanese languages; aged ~85; linguists (Abbi) noted she sang songs. Reports commonly stated that she sang songs in Bo that no one alive understood. I'll present softly.
- Language death rate: often cited "a language dies every two weeks" (Krauss-era); more conservative: several languages endangered; I'll hedge with "depending on who's counting, one dies every few weeks or months."
- Funes details: falls, gains memory via horse accident; crushing totality; quote paraphrase: "To think is to forget differences." Accurate.
- Masons' marks: real historical phenomenon.
- Ebbinghaus: skip or brief mention of curve. Skip to save space.

Also possible inclusion: H.M.? Skip.

Write final with attention to rhythm. Aim ~1000 words. I'll count roughly during composition—paragraphs sized as planned. I'll write it now carefully, keeping it beautiful but restrained.

One more consideration: The user said "write freely," so essay-voice wandering is apt; I shouldn't preface with meta-commentary. Just deliver the piece. Maybe a one-line intro? No—cleanest to just give the piece, perhaps with title. A very brief lead-in isn't needed; diving straight in honors "freely."
